## Today's Learning Goals

::: {.small-text}
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- Outline the modelling framework of the <span style="color: purple;">Ordinal Logistic regression</span>.
- Explain the concept of <span style="color: purple;">proportional odds</span>.
- Fit and interpret Ordinal Logistic regression.
- Use the Ordinal Logistic regression for prediction.
- Assess the assumption of proportional odds via the <span style="color: purple;">Brant-Wald test</span>.
- Contrast the Ordinal Logistic regression models under <span style="color: purple;">proportional and non-proportional odds assumptions</span>.
:::

## 1. The Need for an Ordinal Model

- We will continue with Regression Analysis on <span style="color: purple;">categorical responses</span>. 

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="400" height="400"/>
</center>
</br>

### 1.1. Reminder

- Recall that a <span style="color: purple;">discrete response</span> is considered as categorical if it is of factor-type with more than two categories:

. . .

1. <span style="color: purple;">Nominal.</span> We have categories that do not follow any specific order—for example, the **type of dwelling** according to the Canadian census: *single-detached house*, *semi-detached house*, *row house*, *apartment*, and *mobile home*.

. . .

2. <span style="color: purple;">Ordinal.</span> The categories, in this case, follow a specific order—for example, a **Likert scale** of survey items: *strongly disagree*, *disagree*, *neutral*, *agree*, and *strongly agree*.

### 1.2. A question to start with ...

- Why not just using Mutinomial Logistic regression in the case of an ordinal response?

. . .

- The previous Multinomial Logistic model is <span style="color: purple;">suboptimal</span> for ordinal responses. 

. . .

- Suppose one does not consider the order in the response levels when necessary. In that case, <span style="color: purple;">we might risk losing valuable information when making inference or predictions</span>.
- This valuable information is in the ordinal scale, which could be set up via <span style="color: purple;">cumulative probabilities</span>.


### 1.3. What to do then?

- An alternative logistic regression that suits <span style="color: purple;">ordinal</span> responses. 
- Hence, the existence of the <span style="color: purple;">Ordinal Logistic regression model</span>.

. . .

- We will expand the regression mindmap to include this new model. 
- Note there is a key characteristic called <span style="color: purple;">proportional odds</span> which is reflected on the <span style="color: purple;">data modelling framework</span>.

## 2. College Juniors Dataset

- To illustrate the use of this <span style="color: purple;">generalized linear model (GLM)</span>, let us introduce an adequate dataset.
- The data frame `college_data` was obtained from the webpage of the [UCLA Statistical Consulting Group](https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/r/dae/ordinal-logistic-regression/). 

. . .

- It contains the results of a <span style="color: purple;">survey</span> applied to $n = 400$ college juniors regarding the factors that influence their **decision to apply to graduate school**.

### 2.1. Read data in `R`

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
college_data <- suppressMessages(read_csv("data/college_data.csv"))
college_data
```

### 2.2. A quick look at data!

- The dataset contains the following variables:
  - `decision`: how likely the student will apply to graduate school, <span style="color: purple;">a discrete and ordinal response with three increasing categories</span> (`unlikely`, `somewhat likely`, and `very likely`).
  - `parent_ed`: whether at least one parent has a graduate degree, <span style="color: purple;">a discrete and binary explanatory variable</span> (`Yes` and `No`).
  - `GPA`: the student's current GPA, <span style="color: purple;">a continuous explanatory variable</span>.

### 2.3. A quick data wrangling!

- Variable `decision` will be our response of interest. 
- Before proceeding with our regression analysis, let us set it up as an <span style="color: purple;">ordered factor</span> via function `as.ordered()`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
college_data$decision <- as.ordered(college_data$decision)
college_data$decision <- fct_relevel(college_data$decision,
  c("unlikely", "somewhat likely", "very likely")
)
levels(college_data$decision)
```

### 2.4. Main Statistical Inquiries

- Let us suppose we want to assess the following:
  - Is `decision` statistically related to `parent_ed` and `GPA`?
  - How can we interpret these statistical relationships (<span style="color: purple;">if there are any!</span>)?

## 3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

- Since `decision` is a <span style="color: purple;">discrete ordinal response</span>, we have to be careful about the plots to be used in the EDA.
- To explore the relationship between `decision` and `GPA` , we will use these side-by-side plots: <span style="color: purple;">boxplots</span> and/or <span style="color: purple;">violin plots</span>.

. . .

- `GPA` is on the $y$-axis, and all categories of `decision` are on the $x$-axis. 
- The side-by-side violin plots show the mean of `GPA` by `decision` category in red points.

### Plots!

```{r}
#| echo: false
college_data <- suppressMessages(read_csv("data/college_data.csv"))

college_data_side_boxplots <- college_data |>
  ggplot(aes(decision, GPA)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = decision)) +
  labs(y = "GPA", x = "Decision to Apply to Graduate School") +
  ggtitle("Side-by-Side Boxplots") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 55),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="BuPu")

college_data_side_violin <- college_data |>
  ggplot(aes(decision, GPA)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = decision)) +
  labs(y = "GPA", x = "Decision to Apply to Graduate School") +
  ggtitle("Side-by-Side Violin Plots") +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean, colour = "red", geom = "point",
    shape = 18, size = 11
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 55),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="BuPu")
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 45
#| fig.height: 25
plot_grid(college_data_side_boxplots,
  college_data_side_violin,
  nrow = 1
)
```

### How can we visually explore the relationship between `decision` and `parent_ed`?

- In the case of two categorical explanatory variables, <span style="color: purple;">we can use stacked bar charts.</span>
- Each bar will show the percentages (depicted on the $y$-axis) of college students falling on each ordered category of `decision` with the categories found in `parent_ed` on the $x$-axis. 

### Plots!

```{r}
#| echo: false
college_data_prop_summary <- as.data.frame(xtabs(
  ~ parent_ed +
    decision,
  college_data
) / rowSums(xtabs(
  ~ parent_ed + decision, college_data
)), responseName = "prop")

college_data_stacked_bars <- ggplot(college_data_prop_summary, aes(x = parent_ed, prop, fill = decision)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.7, colour = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(prop >= 0.05, paste0(sprintf("%.0f", prop*100),"%"),"")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), colour = "firebrick3", fontface = "bold", size = 15) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(y = "Percent", x = "Parent Education Status", fill = "") +
  ggtitle("Stacked Bar Charts")  +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 55, angle = 0),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 55, angle = 0),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 45, margin = margin(r = 1, unit = "cm")), 
        legend.title = element_text(size = 45, face = "bold")) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = "Decision")) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues")
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 45
#| fig.height: 25
plot_grid(college_data_side_boxplots,
  college_data_side_violin,
  college_data_stacked_bars,
  nrow = 1
)
```

## 4. Data Modelling Framework

- Let us suppose that a given <span style="color: purple;">discrete ordinal response</span> $Y_i$ (for $i = 1, \dots, n$) has categories $1, 2, \dots, m$ in a training set of size $n$.

> **Heads-up:** Categories $1, 2, \dots, m$ <span style="color: purple;">implicate an ordinal scale here</span>, i.e., $1 < 2 < \dots < m$.

. . .

- Also, note there is more than one class of Ordinal Logistic regression. 
- We will review the <span style="color: purple;">proportional odds</span> model (a <span style="color: purple;">cumulative logit model</span>).

### When $m = 3$

- We will set up an Ordinal Logistical regression model for this specific dataset <span style="color: purple;">with $m = 3$ for the levels of $Y_i$</span>, i.e.,

\begin{gather*}
1 = \texttt{unlikely} \\
2 = \texttt{somewhat likely} \\
3 = \texttt{very likely}
\end{gather*}

### The Regressors

<br>

- For the $i$th observation, we have the continuous $X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}$ and the dummy variable 

::: {.small-text}
$$
X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}} =
\begin{cases}
1 \; \; \; \; \mbox{at least one parent has a graduate degree},\\
0 \; \; \; \; 	\mbox{neither of the parents has a graduate degree.}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

### Then...

<br>

- The model will indicate how each one of the regressors affects the <span style="color: purple;">cumulative logarithm of the odds</span> in `decision` for the following $2$ situations:

::: {.small-text}
\begin{gather*}
\text{Level } \texttt{somewhat likely}  \text{ or any lesser degree versus level } \texttt{very likely} \\
\text{Level } \texttt{unlikely} \text{ versus level } \texttt{somewhat likely} \text{ or any higher degree}
\end{gather*}
:::

### These are our cumulative log-odds!

- We have the following system of $2$ equations:

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{very likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}, X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}\right] \\ &= \beta_0^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})} - \beta_1 X_{i, \texttt{GPA}} - \beta_2 X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{unlikely})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{unlikely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i \geq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}\right] \\ &= \beta_0^{(\texttt{unlikely})} - \beta_1 X_{i, \texttt{GPA}} - \beta_2 X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}.
\end{align*}
:::

### Note the following...

- The system has $2$ intercepts but <span style="color: purple;">only $2$ regression coefficients</span>. 
- Check the signs of the <span style="color: purple;">common</span> $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$, which are minuses. This is a fundamental parameterization of the <span style="color: purple;">proportional odds</span> model.

### Some algebraic manipulation...

- To make coefficient intepretation easier, we could re-expresss the equations of $\eta_i^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})}$  and $\eta_i^{(\texttt{unlikely})}$ as follows:

. . .

::: {.small-text}
\begin{gather*}
\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{very likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i \leq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})} = \\
\exp\big(-\beta_0^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})}\big) \exp\big(\beta_1 X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}\big) \exp\big(\beta_2 X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}\big)
\end{gather*}
\begin{gather*}
\frac{P(Y_i \geq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{unlikely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})} = \\
\exp\big(-\beta_0^{(\texttt{unlikely})}\big) \exp\big(\beta_1 X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}\big) \exp\big(\beta_2 X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}\big).
\end{gather*}
:::

#### Further Insights

- Both regression coefficients ($\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$) have a multiplicative effect on the odds that we have on the left-hand side. 
- Moreover, <span style="color: purple;">given the proportional odds assumptions</span>, the regressor effects are the same for both cumulative odds.

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="250" height="250"/>
</center>
</br>

### What is the math for the general case with $m$ response categories and $k$ regressors?

::: {.small-text}

- This model will indicate how each one of the $k$ regressors $X_{i,1}, \dots, X_{i,k}$ affects the <span style="color: purple;">cumulative logarithm of the odds</span> in the ordinal response (with $m$ levels) for the following $m - 1$ situations:

\begin{gather*}
\text{Level } m - 1 \text{ or any lesser degree versus level } m\\
\text{Level } m - 2 \text{ or any lesser degree versus level } m - 1 \text{ or any higher degree}\\
\vdots \\
\text{Level } 2 \text{ or any lesser degree versus level } 3 \text{ or any higher degree}\\
\text{Level } 1 \text{ versus level } 2 \text{ or any higher degree}\\
\end{gather*}

:::

### Link Functions

<br>

::: {.small-text-v2}
\begin{gather*}
\eta_i^{(m - 1)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq m - 1 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}{P(Y_i = m \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}\right] = \beta_0^{(m - 1)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k} \\
\eta_i^{(m - 2)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq m - 2 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}{P(Y_i > m - 2 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}\right] = \beta_0^{(m - 2)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k} \\
\vdots \\
\eta_i^{(2)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq 2 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}{P(Y_i > 2 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}\right] = \beta_0^{(2)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k} \\
\eta_i^{(1)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = 1 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}{P(Y_i > 1 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}\right] = \beta_0^{(1)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k}.
\end{gather*}
:::

### Cumulative Probabilities

- Note that the previous system has $m - 1$ intercepts but <span style="color: purple;">only $k$ regression coefficients</span>. 
- In general, the previous $m - 1$ equations can be generalized for levels $j = m - 1, \dots, 1$ as follows:

. . .

::: {.small-text}
\begin{gather*}
\eta_i^{(j)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq j \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}{P(Y_i > j \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k})}\right] = \beta_0^{(j)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k} \\
\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \Rightarrow \; P(Y_i \leq j \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0^{(j)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k}\right)}{1 + \exp\left(\beta_0^{(j)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} - \ldots - \beta_k X_{i, k}\right)}.
\end{gather*}
:::

### Standalone Probabilities

::: {.small-text}
- The <span style="color: purple;">standalone probability</span> that $Y_i$ will fall in the category $j$ is computed as follows:
$$
p_{i,j} = P(Y_i = j \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k}) \\
= P(Y_i \leq j \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k}) - P(Y_i \leq j - 1 \mid X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,k}),
$$

- Hence:
$$
P(Y_i = 1) = p_{i,1} \;\;\;\; P(Y_i = 2) = p_{i,2} \;\; \dots \;\; P(Y_i = m) = p_{i,m},
$$

- Where:
$$
\sum_{j = 1}^m p_{i,j} = p_{i,1} + p_{i,2} + \dots + p_{i,m} = 1.
$$
:::

### iClicker Question

::: {.small-text}
- Suppose we have a case with an ordered response of **five levels** and **four continuous regressors**.
- How many link functions, intercepts, and coefficients will our Ordinal Logistic regression model have under a **proportional odds assumption**?

**A.** Four link functions, four intercepts, and sixteen regression coefficients. 

**B.** Five link functions, five intercepts, and five regression coefficients. 

**C.** Five link functions, five intercepts, and twenty regression coefficients. 

**D.** Four link functions, four intercepts, and four regression coefficients. 
:::

<img src="images/panda.png" width="160" height="160"/>
</center>
</br>

### A Graphical Intuition of the Proportional Odds Assumption

- There is an <span style="color: purple;">optional section</span> in the notes that shows mathematically what the proportional odds assumption stands for in the Ordinal Logistic regression model with $k$ regressors and a training set size of $n$, using a response of $m$ levels in general. 

. . .

- That said, let us check the graphical intuition with an example of an ordinal response of $5$ levels and a single continuous regressor $X_{i , 1}$ (<span style="color: purple;">which is unbounded!</span>).

### System of Cumulative Logit Equations

\begin{gather*}
\eta_i^{(4)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq 4 \mid X_{i,1})}{P(Y_i = 5 \mid X_{i,1})}\right] = \beta_0^{(4)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \\
\eta_i^{(3)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq 3 \mid X_{i,1})}{P(Y_i > 3 \mid X_{i,1})}\right] = \beta_0^{(3)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \\
\eta_i^{(2)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq 2 \mid X_{i,1})}{P(Y_i > 2 \mid X_{i,1})}\right] = \beta_0^{(2)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \\
\eta_i^{(1)} = \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = 1 \mid X_{i,1})}{P(Y_i > 1 \mid X_{i,1})}\right] = \beta_0^{(1)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1}.
\end{gather*}

### Some algebraic manipulation...

::: {.small-text}
\begin{gather*}
P(Y_i \leq 4 \mid X_{i,1}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0^{(4)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \right)}{1 + \exp\left(\beta_0^{(4)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1}\right)} \\
P(Y_i \leq 3 \mid X_{i,1}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0^{(3)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \right)}{1 + \exp\left(\beta_0^{(3)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1}\right)} \\
P(Y_i \leq 2 \mid X_{i,1}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0^{(2)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \right)}{1 + \exp\left(\beta_0^{(2)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1}\right)} \\
P(Y_i \leq 1 \mid X_{i,1}) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0^{(1)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1} \right)}{1 + \exp\left(\beta_0^{(1)} - \beta_1 X_{i, 1}\right)}. \\
\end{gather*}
:::

### Note following...

- There are four intercepts $\left( \beta_0^{(1)}, \beta_0^{(2)}, \beta_0^{(3)}, \beta_0^{(4)} \right)$  and a single coefficient $\beta_1$. 
- Let us assume we estimate these five parameters to be the following:
\begin{gather*}
\hat{\beta_0}^{(1)} = 4 \quad \quad \hat{\beta_0}^{(2)} = 5.5 \\ 
\hat{\beta_0}^{(3)} = 6.3 \quad \quad \hat{\beta_0}^{(4)} = 10 \\
\hat{\beta_1} = 12.
\end{gather*}

### The sigmoid functions! 

```{r}
#| echo: false 
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 12.5
library(tidyverse)

x_grid <- seq(-0.5, 1.6, length.out = 1200)
a_vals <- c("k = 4" = 10, "k = 3" = 6.3, "k = 2" = 5.5, "k = 1" = 4)

df <- map_dfr(names(a_vals), \(nm) {
  a <- a_vals[[nm]]
  tibble(
    x = x_grid,
    y = plogis(a - 12 * x),
    curve = nm
  )
}) |>
  mutate(curve = factor(curve, levels = names(a_vals)))

eq_df <- tibble(
  curve = factor(names(a_vals), levels = names(a_vals)),
  x = 1.58,
  y = c(0.95, 0.8, 0.65, 0.5),
  lab = c(
    "P(Y[i] <= 4 ~ '|' ~ X[i,1])==frac(e^{10-12*x},1+e^{10-12*x})",
    "P(Y[i] <= 3 ~ '|' ~ X[i,1])==frac(e^{6.3-12*x},1+e^{6.3-12*x})",
    "P(Y[i] <= 2 ~ '|' ~ X[i,1])==frac(e^{5.5-12*x},1+e^{5.5-12*x})",
    "P(Y[i] <= 1 ~ '|' ~ X[i,1])==frac(e^{4-12*x},1+e^{4-12*x})"
  )
)

cb_pal <- c(
  "k = 4" = "#0072B2",
  "k = 3" = "#D55E00",
  "k = 2" = "#009E73",
  "k = 1" = "#CC79A7"
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(
    data = eq_df,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = lab, color = curve),
    hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, parse = TRUE,
    size = 7.5,         
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cb_pal) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.5, 1.6), ylim = c(0, 1.05)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Cumulative Probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 21)
  )
```



## 5. Estimation

::: {.small-text}
- Estimates are obtained through <span style="color: purple;">maximum likelihood</span>, where we also assume a <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial joint probability mass function</span> of the $n$ responses $Y_i$ via cumulative probabilities in the joint likelihood function.
:::
. . .

::: {.small-text}
- To fit the model with the package `MASS`, we use `polr()`. 
The argument `Hess = TRUE` is required to compute the [Hessian matrix](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Hessian.html) of the <span style="color: purple;">log-likelihood function</span>, which is used to obtain the standard errors of the estimates.
:::


```{webr}
#| autorun: true
ordinal_model <- polr(formula = decision ~ parent_ed + GPA,
  data = college_data, Hess = TRUE
)
```

## 6. Inference

- We also use the <span style="color: purple;">Wald statistic</span> $z_j = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j}{\mbox{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)}$ to test the hypotheses:
\begin{gather*}
H_0: \beta_j = 0\\
H_a: \beta_j \neq 0.
\end{gather*}

- Provided the sample size $n$ is large enough, $z_j$ has an <span style="color: purple;">approximately Standard Normal distribution</span> under $H_0$.

### Code in `R`!

::: {.small-text}
- Terms `unlikely|somewhat likely` and `somewhat likely|very likely` refer to $\hat{\beta_0}^{(\texttt{unlikely})}$ and $\hat{\beta_0}^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})}$, respectively.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
summary_ordinal_model <- cbind(tidy(ordinal_model), p.value = pnorm(abs(tidy(ordinal_model)$statistic), lower.tail = FALSE) * 2
) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 2)
summary_ordinal_model
```

### Using $\alpha = 0.05$

- We see that those coefficients associated with `GPA` and `parent_ed` are statistically significant with $\alpha = 0.05$.
- Function `confint()` can provide the 95% confidence intervals for the estimates contained in `ordinal_model`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
round(confint(ordinal_model), 2)
```

## 7. Coefficient Interpretation

- The interpretation of the Ordinal Logistic regression coefficients will change since we are modelling cumulative probabilities. 
- Let us interpret the association of `decision` with `GPA` and `parent_ed`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
tibble(summary_ordinal_model[1:2, 1:2], exp.estimate = round(exp(summary_ordinal_model[1:2, 2]), 2))
```

### Interpretations

- By using the column `exp.estimate`, <span style="color: purple;">along with the model equations on the original scale of the cumulative odds</span>, we interpret the two regression coefficients above <span style="color: purple;">by each odds</span> as follows:
- For the odds:

$$\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{very likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i \leq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})} = \\ \exp\big(-\beta_0^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})}\big) \exp\big(\beta_1 X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}\big) \exp\big(\beta_2 X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}\big).$$

### We have ...

::: {.small-text}
> $\beta_1$: "for each one-unit increase in the `GPA`, the odds that the student is `very likely`  versus `somewhat likely` or `unlikely` to apply to graduate school increase by $\exp \left( \hat{\beta}_1 \right) = 1.82$ times (while holding `parent_ed` constant)."
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> $\beta_2$: "for those respondents whose parents attended to graduate school, the odds that the student is `very likely` versus `somewhat likely` or `unlikely` to apply to graduate school increase by $\exp \left( \hat{\beta}_2 \right) = 2.86$ times (when compared to those respondents whose parents did not attend to graduate school and holding `GPA` constant)."
:::

### And...

- For the odds: 

$$\frac{P(Y_i \geq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{unlikely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})} = \\ \exp\big(-\beta_0^{(\texttt{unlikely})}\big) \exp\big(\beta_1 X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}\big) \exp\big(\beta_2 X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}\big).$$

### We have ...

::: {.small-text}
> $\beta_1$: "for each one-unit increase in the `GPA`, the odds that the student is `very likely` or `somewhat likely` versus `unlikely` to apply to graduate school increase by $\exp \left( \hat{\beta}_1 \right) = 1.82$ times (while holding `parent_ed` constant)."
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> $\beta_2$: "for those respondents whose parents attended to graduate school, the odds that the student is `very likely`  or `somewhat likely` versus `unlikely` to apply to graduate school increase by $\exp \left( \hat{\beta}_2 \right) = 2.86$ times (when compared to those respondents whose parents did not attend to graduate school and holding `GPA` constant)."
:::

## 8. Predictions

- <span style="color: purple;">Aside from our main statistical inquiries</span>, using the function `predict()` with the object `ordinal_model`, we can obtain the estimated probabilities to apply to graduate school (associated to `unlikely`, `somewhat likely`, and `very likely`) for a student with a `GPA` of 3.5 whose parents attended to graduate school.

. . .

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
round(predict(ordinal_model, tibble(GPA = 3.5, parent_ed = "Yes"), type = "probs"), 2)
```

### Thus...

- We can see that it is `somewhat likely` to apply to graduate school with a probability of 0.48. 
- <span style="color: purple;">Thus, we could classify the student in this ordinal category.</span>

## 9. Model Selection

- <span style="color: purple;">To perform model selection</span>, we can use the same techniques from `lecture2`. That said, some `R` coding functions might not be entirely available for the `polr()` models. 
- Still, these statistical techniques and metrics can be manually coded.

## 10. Non-proportional Odds

- Now, we might wonder:

> *What happens if we do not fulfil the proportional odds assumption in our Ordinal Logistic regression model?*

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="300" height="300"/>
</center>
</br>

### 10.1. The Brant-Wald Test

::: {.small-text}
- The Ordinal Logistic model under the proportional odds assumption is <span style="color: purple;">the first step</span> when performing Regression Analysis on an ordinal response. 
- Once this model has been fitted, <span style="color: purple;">it is possible to assess whether it fulfils this strong assumption statistically</span>.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- We can do it via the **Brant-Wald test**.
- This tool performs statistically assesses whether our model globally fulfils this assumption:
\begin{gather*}
H_0: \text{Our Ordinal Logistic regression model globally} \\ \text{fulfils the proportional odds assumption.} \\
H_a: \text{Otherwise}.
\end{gather*}
:::

#### Regressor-specifc Tests

<br>

- It also performs further hypothesis testing on each regressor. 
- With $k$ regressors for $j = 1, \dots, k$; we have the following hypotheses:
\begin{gather*}
H_0: \text{The } j \text{th regressor in our Ordinal Logistic regression} \\ \text{model fulfils the proportional odds assumption.} \\
H_a: \text{Otherwise}.
\end{gather*}

### 10.2. Code in `R`!

- Function `brant()` from package `brant` implements this tool, which can be used in our `polr()` object `ordinal_model`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
brant(ordinal_model)
```


#### Notes on Output

- The row `Omnibus` represents the global model, while the other two rows correspond to our two regressors: `parent_ed` and `GPA`. 
- With $\alpha = 0.05$, **we are completely fulfilling the proportional odds assumption** (the column `probability` delivers the corresponding $p$-values).

. . .

> **Heads-up:** The Brant Wald test essentially compares this basic Ordinal Logistic regression model of $m - 1$ cumulative logit functions (i.e., the ordinal response has $m$ categories) versus a set of $m − 1$ correlated Binary Logistic regressions.

### 10.3. A Non-proportional Odds Model

::: {.small-text}
- Suppose that our example case <span style="color: purple;">does not fulfil</span> the proportional odds assumption according to the Brant Wald test. 
- It is possible to have a model under a <span style="color: purple;">non-proportional odds assumption</span>:
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i \leq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{very likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}}, X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}\right] \\ &= \beta_0^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})} - \beta_1^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})} X_{i, \texttt{GPA}} - \\ & \qquad \beta_2^{(\texttt{somewhat likely})} X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{unlikely})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{unlikely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}{P(Y_i \geq \texttt{somewhat likely} \mid X_{i, \texttt{GPA}},X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}})}\right] \\ &= \beta_0^{(\texttt{unlikely})} - \beta_1^{(\texttt{unlikely})} X_{i, \texttt{GPA}} - \beta_2^{(\texttt{unlikely})} X_{i, \texttt{parent_ed}}.
\end{align*}
:::

#### Generalized Ordinal Logistic Regression Model

<br>

- This class of models can be fit via [**the function `cumulative()`**](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/VGAM/html/cumulative.html) from package `VGAM`. 
- Note that estimation, inference, coefficient interpretation, and predictions are conducted in a similar way <span style="color: purple;">compared to the proportional odds model</span>. 

### In-class Question

- Why would we have to be cautious when fitting a non-proportional odds model in the context of a response with a considerable number of ordinal levels and regressors?

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="350" height="350"/>
</center>
</br>

## 11. Wrapping Up on Categorical Regression Models

::: {.small-text-v2}
- Multinomial and Ordinal Logistic regression models address cases where our response is <span style="color: purple;">discrete and categorical</span>. 
- These models are <span style="color: purple;">another class GLMs</span>.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text-v2}
- <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial Logistic regression</span> approaches <span style="color: purple;">nominal responses</span>. It heavily relies on a baseline response level and the odds' natural logarithm.
- <span style="color: purple;">Ordinal Logistic regression</span> approaches <span style="color: purple;">ordinal responses</span>. It relies on cumulative odds on an ordinal scale.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text-v2}
- We have to be careful with <span style="color: purple;">coefficient interpretations</span> in these models, especially with the cumulative odds. This will imply an <span style="color: purple;">effective communication</span> of these estimated models for inferential matters.
:::
